newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine official says no harvest bottleneck.
newsitem.headline: Argentine official says no harvest bottleneck.

text.p: Big investments in ports and storage capacity will enable Argentina to avoid bottlenecks this season even if farmers, as widely expected, harvest a record 50 million tonnes of grain, a top official said Tuesday.

"We have to end the myth that when Argentina has a big crop it has to sell it off at any price because it does not have storage capacity. Today this is absolutely false," Undersecretary for Food Felix Cirio told a seminar on grains storage in Buenos Aires.
"There have been very significant investments in ports and in harvest infrastructure and today we have an installed (storage) capacity of around 46 million tonnes," said Cirio.

He said the wheat harvest alone should provide an export surplus of nine million to 10 million tonnes, more than double last year's. The wheat will be exported to a wide range of countries, unlike last season when Brazil bought the bulk.
Traders are predicting that wheat output will be 14 million tonnes or over, compared with just over 9.2 million in 1995/96. Overall grain output may jump to 50 million tonnes.

"Argentina is about to have a big harvest, and I believe that we are going to continue having big harvests," Cirio said. He added that government figures show that moisture levels in most wheat areas are among the best in 15 years.

Argentina is only now completing the green revolution which swept most of the world 20 years ago. Although farmers adopted improved seed varieties back in the 1970s, they are only now beginning to use fertilizer, which for years was uneconomical because of Argentina's long-distorted economy.
The government believes Argentine farmers will use from 1.8 million to two million tonnes of fertilizer this season, up from only 300,000 tonnes five years ago, Cirio said.
The economic stability since the governemnt pegged the local peso at par with the dollar in 1991 and big cuts in import duties have also permitted farmers to boost investments in equipment.

But Cirio chided the grain trade and farmers for their slowness in embracing futures markets, long regarded with suspicion in Argentina. Argentine producers still sell only a fraction of their output on the Buenos Aires Futures Exchange, leaving them at the mercy of increasingly volatile international markets.

"I don't see a pressure of supply of services from the grains business, nor demand from the producers for the new services, in keeping with the amount of money involved, in keeping with the importance the farm business has today," Cirio said.
He called on local elevators, cooperatives and grains traders to expand their portfolio of futures and offer services such as warrants.
Things are changing, but slowly. Local business in grains warrants will total $1 billion this year, he said.
The government is holding over 30 seminars a year to educate farmers and the grain trade about futures instruments.
